nodes.name: Coprecipitation synthesis of NiNi-PBA
nodes.procedure: Ni(H2O)2[Ni(CN)4] PBA (NiNi-PBA) nanoplates are first synthesized through a facile coprecipitation method and used as the templates.
nodes.source_text: Ni(H2O)2[Ni(CN)4] PBA (NiNi-PBA) nanoplates are first synthesized through a facile coprecipitation method40 and used as the templates.

nodes.name: Ion exchange to Ni(OH)2
nodes.procedure: Ni(OH)2 porous nanoplates are obtained by the reaction between the NiNi-PBA precursors and NaOH solution (2.0 M), which is driven by the high concentration of hydroxide ions. In the alkaline solution, an ion exchange reaction takes place: Ni(H2O)2[Ni(CN)4](s) + 2OH−(aq.) → Ni(OH)2(s) + Ni(CN)42−(aq.).
nodes.source_text: Ni(OH)2 porous nanoplates are obtained by the reaction between the NiNi-PBA precursors and NaOH solution (2.0 M)...

unit_operations.name: Ion Exchange
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: reaction between the NiNi-PBA precursors and NaOH solution (2.0 M)

nodes.name: Calcination to NiO
nodes.procedure: The as-synthesized NiNi-PBA nanoplates are calcinated in an air atmosphere to prepare nanoporous NiO nanoplates.
nodes.source_text: The as-synthesized NiNi-PBA nanoplates are calcinated in an air atmosphere to prepare nanoporous NiO nanoplates.

nodes.name: Low-temperature phosphidation to Ni–P
nodes.procedure: Ni–P porous nanoplates are fabricated through low-temperature phosphidation of NiNi-PBA templates under an argon atmosphere. After the low-temperature phosphidation of the NiNi-PBA nanoplates, the product is composed of a mixture of Ni5P4 (JCPDS no. 18-883) and Ni2P (JCPDS no. 65-1989) with Ni2P as the major component.
nodes.source_text: Ni–P porous nanoplates are fabricated through low-temperature phosphidation of NiNi-PBA templates under an argon atmosphere.

unit_operations.name: Phosphidation
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: low-temperature phosphidation of NiNi-PBA templates under an argon atmosphere

nodes.description: OER stability testing in 1.0 M KOH
nodes.source_text: Only a little anodic current loss is observed for Ni–P nanoplates after 1000 continuous cycles at an accelerated scanning rate of 20 mV s⁻¹. The I–t measurement further reveals that they can maintain good catalytic activity for at least 10 h in alkaline solution.

to achieve a current density of 10 mA cm⁻², the Ni–P nanoplate electrocatalyst only requires an overpotential of 110 mV... The Tafel slope of Ni–P nanoplates is 73 mV dec⁻¹... the superior durability of the electrocatalytic response for HER is confirmed by cycling the Ni–P nanoplate electrode continuously for 1000 cycles.

nodes.source_text: when the Nyquist plots of Ni–P, Ni(OH)₂, and NiO nanoplates are compared at the same overpotential (180 mV), the Ni–P nanoplates show much lower R_ct values than Ni(OH)₂ and NiO nanoplates

nodes.characterization_summary: All diffraction peaks assigned to Hofmann-type Ni(H2O)2[Ni(CN)4]·xH2O with 2D layered structure, no impurity peaks detected.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The formation of NiNi-PBA is confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis... No additional peaks from impurities are detected, indicating the high purity of the product.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiNi-PBA nanoplates show 2D plate-like morphology with lateral sizes 300-400 nm and thickness 40-50 nm, smooth surface confirming single-crystalline nature.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) image shows that all the products exhibit a 2D plate-like morphology... confirming the single-crystalline nature.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiNi-PBA nanoplates show dense nature without discernible porosity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image clearly demonstrates its dense nature without discernible porosity.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni–P composed of mixture of Ni5P4 (JCPDS no. 18-883) and Ni2P (JCPDS no. 65-1989) with Ni2P as major component (Fig. S1, ESI†).
nodes.evidence_snippet: After the low-temperature phosphidation of the NiNi-PBA nanoplates, the product is composed of a mixture of Ni5P4 (JCPDS no. 18-883) and Ni2P (JCPDS no. 65-1989) (Fig. S1, ESI†), with Ni2P as the major component.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni–P maintains 2D morphology with rough surface and highly porous nature.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Following phosphidation, the FESEM image shows that the 2D morphology is well maintained while the surface of the nanoplates becomes rough... reveals the highly porous nature of Ni–P nanoplates.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni–P nanoplates show rough and porous feature, covered by amorphous carbon layer 2-3 nm thick.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Fig. 3c and d show the FESEM and TEM images of one single Ni–P nanoplate, respectively, confirming its rough and porous feature... The high-resolution TEM image further verifies that nickel phosphides are covered by an amorphous carbon layer with a thickness of around 2-3 nm.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni and P elements uniformly distributed throughout Ni–P nanoplate, atomic ratio Ni:P = 21:17, carbon content 30.9 wt%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental mapping images further demonstrate that both Ni and P elements are uniformly distributed throughout the whole nanoplate. The corresponding EDX spectrum shows the atomic ratio between Ni and P to be 21:17 and the existence of high content of carbon (30.9 wt%) in the nanoplate.

nodes.characterization_summary: Carbon coated nickel phosphides porous nanoplates exhibit specific surface area of 35 m² g⁻¹.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The as-synthesized carbon coated nickel phosphides porous nanoplates exhibit a specific surface area of 35 m² g⁻¹.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiO diffraction peaks indexed to cubic phase (JCPDS no. 04-0835), no impurity peaks (Fig. S5a, ESI†).
nodes.evidence_snippet: All the diffraction peaks of the calcinated products can be indexed to the cubic phase of NiO (JCPDS no. 04-0835) (Fig. S5a, ESI†). No other peaks from impurity are observed.

nodes.characterization_summary: C–N stretching peaks at 2170 cm⁻¹ disappear after NiNi-PBA reaction with NaOH, indicating removal of Ni(CN)₄²⁻.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The ion exchange reaction between NiNi-PBA and NaOH is verified by Fourier transform-infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR). The peaks of C–N stretching located at 2170 cm⁻¹ disappear after the reaction.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni(OH)₂ confirmed by Ni 2p1/2 at 873.4 eV and 2p3/2 at 855.6 eV (spin-energy separation 17.8 eV); O 1s shows peaks at 529.9 eV (metal–oxygen), 531.2 eV (OH⁻), 532.5 eV (adsorbed water).
nodes.evidence_snippet: XPS analysis is performed to confirm the successful synthesis of Ni(OH)₂. The typical Ni 2p1/2 and 2p3/2 peaks ... at 873.4 and 855.6 eV, respectively. The spin-energy separation of 17.8 eV is the characteristic of the Ni(OH)₂ phase.

nodes.characterization_summary: NiO nanoplates show highly porous structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: TEM observation reveals the highly porous structure of NiO nanoplates (Fig. S5d, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: NiO preserves plate-like morphology after calcination.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The plate-like morphology is well preserved after calcination (Fig. S5b and c, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni(OH)2 retains plate-like morphology with porous structure after ion exchange.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The as-prepared Ni(OH)2 product retains the plate-like morphology with porous structure after ion exchange (Fig. S6e and f, ESI†).
